prompt: What problem was service-oriented architecture first meant to solve?
hint: Large companies around the year 2000.

choices.text: Applications that could not talk to each other
choices.why: Right: expose each one's capabilities through a published contract.

choices.text: Websites that were too slow to load on mobile phones
choices.why: Mobile performance was not the problem of the time.

choices.text: Programs too large for one server's memory
choices.why: SOA was about integration, not memory.

choices.text: The cost of software licences per processor
choices.why: Licensing was not what SOA addressed.

prompt: Five applications are joined point to point, each to every other. How many links is that?
What does the lesson name as the part of the ESB that went wrong?
hint: Where did the rules of the business end up?

choices.text: Translating between the data formats of different applications
choices.why: That was real, useful work.

choices.text: Cutting the number of connections
choices.why: Fewer connections was a benefit.

choices.text: Business processes written in the bus, owned by a central team
choices.why: Right. Every change queued behind every other team's change.

choices.text: Using HTTP as a transport
choices.why: SOAP often used HTTP, and that was not the trouble.

prompt: Match each term to what it is.
hint: The first two paragraphs and the bus.

pairs.right: an XML description of a service's operations
a central product every message passed through

prompt: What is the main lesson microservices took from SOA's experience with the bus?
hint: Smart endpoints, dumb pipes.

choices.text: Never use a message queue between services
choices.why: Queues are fine; they carry messages and decide nothing.

choices.text: Keep business rules out of the middleware between services
choices.why: Right. Rules in the pipe make every team depend on the pipe's owners.

choices.text: Replace XML with JSON everywhere, including the database
choices.why: The format was a detail; the lesson is about where the logic lives.

choices.text: Put every service behind one central registry
choices.why: A central registry was SOA's governance, not the lesson.

prompt: In a system of microservices, orchestration is allowed. What makes it different from orchestration in an ESB?
hint: Who owns the orchestrator?

choices.text: It runs faster because it uses JSON
choices.why: Speed and format are not the difference.

choices.text: It is forbidden to call more than two services
choices.why: There is no such limit.

choices.text: It never fails, because it is stateless
choices.why: An orchestrator can fail like anything else, and holds state about the process.

choices.text: It is a service owned by the team that owns the process
choices.why: Right, not a shared product owned by somebody else.

prompt: Match each row of the comparison to SOA as practised or to microservices.
hint: The table at the top of the section.

pairs.left: each service on its team's schedule

prompt: When each service reacts to the others' events and nobody holds the whole flow, the style is called ___.
hint: The opposite of orchestration.

prompt: What does "serverless" mean, in the sense of functions as a service?
hint: There is a server. Who sees it?

choices.text: The code runs in the user's browser
choices.why: That would be client-side code, not FaaS.

choices.text: No machine is involved at any point
choices.why: There is always a machine; the platform hides it.

choices.text: You never see or run the server; the platform does
choices.why: Right. You hand over a function and pay for the time it ran.

choices.text: The function has no access to a network
choices.why: Functions call APIs and databases all the time.

prompt: Using the lesson's handler, what fee in cents does a basket of 7,400 g pay?
hint: 790, plus 150 for each started kilogram over 5 kg.

prompt: Which of Quitanda's jobs fits a function best?
hint: Short work, triggered by something else, nothing kept in between.

choices.text: Holding a live connection to each courier's phone all day
choices.why: Long-held connections do not fit a function; lesson 18.

choices.text: Expiring unpaid orders every night at 02:00
choices.why: Right: a short scheduled job with nothing to keep.

choices.text: A two-hour import of the full catalogue history
choices.why: Function platforms stop an invocation long before two hours.

choices.text: The shop's checkout under steady all-day load
choices.why: Steady load is where an always-on server tends to be cheaper.

prompt: Why must a handler keep nothing in memory that the next call relies on?
hint: Which copy answers the next event, and does it exist?

choices.text: Whichever copy the platform picks takes the next event
choices.why: Right. The platform starts and stops copies as it pleases.

choices.text: Memory is billed at a higher rate than compute time on every platform
choices.why: Billing is not the reason; memory is part of the GB-s price.

choices.text: Python deletes global variables after each call
choices.why: Python does nothing of the kind.

choices.text: The handler would become too slow to start
choices.why: Start-up time is about loading, not about what is kept.

prompt: In the lab, what did the cold call pay for that the warm calls did not?
hint: The handler was the same in both.

choices.text: A slower version of the handler
choices.why: The handler was the same few lines.

choices.text: A larger event
choices.why: The event was the same, `{"weight_g": 7400}`.

choices.text: Creating a container and starting the interpreter
choices.why: Right: everything before the handler.

choices.text: Sending the answer over HTTP to a browser instead of to a terminal
choices.why: The cold path printed to the terminal; HTTP was the warm path.

prompt: The lab's cold call took 0.741 s and a warm call 0.0026 s. Roughly how many times longer was the cold call? Round to the nearest ten.
hint: Divide one by the other.

prompt: A team keeps a minimum of instances that never stop, to avoid cold starts. What has it bought, in effect?
hint: Paying while nothing runs.

choices.text: A faster handler
choices.why: The handler runs at the same speed; only the wait before it goes.

choices.text: An always-on server, in smaller pieces
choices.why: Right. AWS sells it as provisioned concurrency.

choices.text: A free tier that never runs out, however many requests arrive
choices.why: Kept-warm instances are billed while idle.

choices.text: Immunity from the platform's run-time limits
choices.why: Limits on run time still apply.

prompt: Which of these make a cold start longer? Choose all that apply.
hint: The table of factors.

choices.text: A runtime that loads and compiles classes before running
choices.why: Right, as the JVM does.

choices.text: Large libraries imported at start-up
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Opening database connections at import time
choices.why: Right: it runs on every cold start.

choices.text: A short handler
choices.why: The handler runs after the start, whatever its length.

prompt: A function with 1,024 MB runs for 500 ms. How many GB-seconds does one call use?
hint: Memory in GB times duration in seconds.

prompt: At US$ 0.20 per million requests, what do 3 million requests cost, before the free allowance?
hint: The requests row of the worked month.

prompt: Above the break-even volume, which is cheaper, and for what kind of traffic especially?
hint: Where do the lines cross, and which keeps rising?

choices.text: Functions, especially for steady traffic
choices.why: Above the crossing, the per-request line is the higher one.

choices.text: Both cost the same at any volume once it is passed
choices.why: They are equal only at the crossing.

choices.text: The always-on server, especially for steady traffic
choices.why: Right. The flat line stays put while the other rises.

choices.text: Functions, especially for bursty traffic
choices.why: Bursts favour functions below the crossing, not above it.

prompt: A burst makes the platform start a thousand copies of a function, each opening its own database connection. What is the risk?
hint: The database has a limit too.

choices.text: The bill doubles because connections are billed per second
choices.why: Connections are not a billing item in the lesson.

choices.text: The database runs out of connections
choices.why: Right. Functions move the operational cost; they do not delete it.

choices.text: The functions all share one connection and queue behind it
choices.why: Each copy holds its own.

choices.text: Cold starts disappear, because the copies are already warm
choices.why: The burst creates copies, which is when cold starts happen.

prompt: In a service mesh, what is the data plane?
hint: What carries every byte?

choices.text: The database every service shares
choices.why: A mesh says nothing about databases.

choices.text: The control plane's configuration store
choices.why: That is part of the control plane.

choices.text: The proxies beside each service
choices.why: Right. Every request passes through them.

choices.text: The network cables between the machines
choices.why: The planes are software, not hardware.

prompt: The stock service needs to know that a call really comes from the shop. Which mesh feature gives that, without TLS code in either program?
hint: Both sides check a certificate.

choices.text: Traffic splitting
choices.why: That sends a share of calls to a new version.

choices.text: Retries
choices.why: Retries resend failed calls; they prove nothing about the caller.

choices.text: Uniform metrics
choices.why: Metrics count calls; they do not authenticate them.

choices.text: Mutual TLS
choices.why: Right. Each proxy holds a certificate naming its service, and both sides check.

prompt: Without a mesh, a call goes straight from the shop to stock. With a mesh, how many proxies does that one call pass through?
hint: Out through one, in through the other.

prompt: Why does the lesson call a mesh more machinery than system for Quitanda's two services?
hint: Who would otherwise write the retry logic, and how many times?

choices.text: Meshes only work with more than ten services
choices.why: There is no such minimum; it is a question of value.

choices.text: Python services cannot run beside a proxy
choices.why: A proxy works with any language; that is its point.

choices.text: Its cost is earned when many teams would repeat the same chores, not with two services
choices.why: Right. A proxy per service and a control plane cost more than they save here.

choices.text: A mesh removes the need for timeouts, which the shop already has
choices.why: A mesh moves timeouts into the proxy; it does not remove the need.

prompt: Quitanda must integrate with a supplier's thirty-year-old ordering system that nobody is allowed to change. Which shape from the table answers that force?
hint: Integrating applications that cannot be changed much.

choices.text: A service mesh
choices.why: A mesh handles network chores between services you run.

choices.text: An integration layer in the SOA tradition
choices.why: Right: that is the force SOA was built for, kept dumb where it can be.

choices.text: Serverless functions for the whole shop
choices.why: Functions are glue; they do not answer the integration by themselves.

choices.text: Splitting the shop's monolith into more services
choices.why: Splitting the shop does not change the supplier's system.

prompt: A nightly import of a supplier's price list takes about an hour. Why does it not fit a function on AWS Lambda?
hint: A limit decides it before the bill does.

choices.text: It runs at night, when functions are scaled to zero
choices.why: Scaling to zero means none run until an event; a schedule is an event.

choices.text: At most 15 minutes per run
choices.why: Right. Lambda stops an invocation after at most 15 minutes, and that limit settles it.

choices.text: Functions cannot read files
choices.why: Reading a file from storage is a common trigger.

choices.text: Price lists are too large to hold in memory
choices.why: The size is not the problem the lesson names.

prompt: Order these shapes by how much of the network chores they take away from each service's own code, least first.
hint: Who writes the timeouts and the TLS in each one?
trap: The monolith comes first only because there is nothing to take away: it has no calls between services at all.
items: A monolith, with no network inside to handle
Microservices, each writing its own timeouts and TLS
Microservices with a mesh, the proxies doing them

prompt: Quitanda's confirmation e-mails are sent after each order: about 40,000 a month, in bursts at lunch and dinner. Which shape fits, and why?
hint: Volume, shape of the load, and whether anybody waits.

choices.text: A service mesh, for mutual TLS to the mail server
choices.why: Encryption to a mail server does not need a mesh, and the shape is the question.

choices.text: An always-on server sized for dinner
choices.why: It works, and it pays for the flat line all day for a few bursts.

choices.text: A function triggered by an order event
choices.why: Right: low volume, bursts, and nobody notices a cold start on an e-mail.

choices.text: A new microservice with its own database and team
choices.why: A team and a database for a few lines of glue is the bill without the force.

prompt: Which statement about the five shapes does the lesson support?
hint: The first paragraph of the last section.

choices.text: Each shape is the next stage of the one before it in time
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite.

choices.text: A system must choose exactly one shape
choices.why: A real system usually mixes them.

choices.text: Each answers a different force, and systems mix them
choices.why: Right. Quitanda could use three at once.

choices.text: Serverless replaces the need for any other shape
choices.why: Its limits settle many cases against it.
